name: REST APIs in Practice
author: Recurse
subject: swe
description: Design and call REST APIs: resources, status codes, pagination, auth, rate limits, fetch and requests, GraphQL and gRPC.

lesson.intro: Almost all software at work talks to an API: frontend to backend, backend to Stripe, GitHub or another team. Learn to design REST APIs others find predictable, and to call them without ignored errors, missing timeouts or retries that charge a card twice.
objectives: Design resource URLs with the right method and status code
Use idempotence to decide which requests are safe to retry
Choose sessions, bearer tokens, API keys or OAuth for a client
Call APIs from Python and JavaScript with timeouts, status checks and backoff
Compare REST with GraphQL and gRPC

sections.title: Resources, URLs and methods
sections.key: REST names resources with plural nouns and lets the method say the action; GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, so they can be retried, while POST is not.
sections.body:
A shop's first API often looks like `/getOrders`, `/createOrder`, `/cancelOrderById?id=42`: every endpoint is a surprise. REST organizes it around **resources** (nouns), with the HTTP **method** as the verb.

- A collection is a plural noun, `/orders`; one item adds its id, `/orders/42`.
- Nest one level only, to show ownership: `/customers/7/orders`.
- Lowercase and hyphens (`/shipping-addresses`); no verbs or file extensions.

[[visual]]

**Safe** methods only read, so crawlers and caches call them freely. **Idempotent** methods have the same effect on the server sent once or five times. That is about server state, not the response: a second `DELETE /orders/42` may get 404 instead of 204, and DELETE is still idempotent. After a timeout, only idempotent requests are safe to resend.

visual.title: Methods on orders
rows: Create an order; the server picks the id

sections.tip: Actions that do not fit create, read, update and delete can become sub-resources: `POST /orders/42/refunds` reads better than `POST /refundOrder`.
sections.pitfall: Using GET for anything that changes data, such as `GET /orders/42/delete`. Link previews, browser prefetching and crawlers will call it for you.

activity.title: Talk to a REST API
activity.prompt: List the tasks with GET, then create one with POST and find the 201 status and the Location header in the response. Fetch the new task by its id, mark it done with PATCH, and delete it. Finally GET it again: the 404 proves the delete worked, and a repeated DELETE would leave the server in exactly that same state.

check.question: A mobile app on a flaky connection sends `PUT /users/7/email` with the same body three times. What is the end result on the server?
choices: Three email-change records are created, one per request
The second and third requests fail with 409 Conflict
The email is set to the new value, exactly as if it had been sent once
The server must reject the repeats unless an idempotency key is sent
check.explanation: PUT is idempotent: setting the email to the same value three times leaves the same state as doing it once. Idempotency keys are needed for non-idempotent requests such as POST, not for PUT.

sections.title: Status codes that matter
sections.key: Return the most specific status a client can act on: 401 means authenticate, 403 means not allowed, 422 means fix the fields, and 429 or 503 mean wait and retry.
sections.body:
Your frontend shows "Something went wrong" for every failure, and support tickets pile up. Status codes let a client react without parsing text: retry later, log in, highlight a field or give up.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

A POST that creates something returns **201** with a `Location` header naming the new resource; a DELETE usually returns **204**. A 200 with `{"error": "not found"}` breaks every client, cache, retry policy and dashboard that trusts status codes.

visual.title: Codes you will meet every week
rows: Success; the body has the result
POST made something; `Location` points to it
Success, nothing to send back (typical for DELETE)
Your cached copy is still current
Not authenticated: missing, expired or bad credentials
Authenticated, but not allowed to do this
No such resource (or you may not know it exists)
Method not allowed on this path; unsupported Content-Type
Clashes with current state: duplicate, stale version
Overloaded or down for now: retry later

visual.title: Pairs that trip people up
rows: 401: I do not know who you are, so refresh the token or log in again. 403: I know you, and no; logging in changes nothing. "Unauthorized" really means unauthenticated
400: the request is malformed. 422: it parses, but values fail validation, such as an email without @. Pick one convention
500: a bug; retrying rarely helps, so retry at most once or twice. 503: temporary, often with `Retry-After`; retry with backoff
Permanent (browsers may cache it) vs temporary. 307 and 308 also keep the method and body
Only after a conditional request: `If-None-Match` with the cached ETag still matches

sections.tip: When unsure, ask what the client should do next. Different next steps (fix the body, log in, wait, give up) deserve different codes.
sections.pitfall: Returning 200 for everything and putting the real outcome in the body. Clients, caches, retry logic and dashboards all look at the status code first.

activity.title: Make it fail on purpose
activity.prompt: Trigger each error on purpose: broken JSON or a task without a title (400), an id that does not exist (404), a method the path does not support (405), and a body sent without Content-Type: application/json (415). For each response, decide what a well-behaved client should do next: fix the request, retry later, or give up.

check.question: A user's token is valid and they can view a shared project (read-only access), but they send a DELETE for it. Which status fits best?
choices: 401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
409 Conflict
400 Bad Request
check.explanation: The server knows who the user is (so not 401) and the request is well-formed (so not 400). The user simply lacks permission to delete, which is exactly what 403 means.

sections.title: JSON bodies and one error shape
sections.key: Keep JSON bodies predictable, with one key style, UTC timestamps, integer money and wrapped lists, and return every error in one shape such as Problem Details.
sections.body:
Open the network tab of any web app: most traffic is JSON, and the bodies are where an API's consistency pays off or falls apart.

[[visual]]

Every error from every endpoint should share one shape, so clients write one handler, not fifty. A common standard is **Problem Details** (RFC 9457), sent as `application/problem+json` with a matching 4xx or 5xx status, never 200. A 422 validation failure:

[[code]]

`type` is a stable identifier to branch on, `title` and `detail` are for humans, and `errors` lets a form mark each bad field. Never make clients match on the human text. Keep stack traces, SQL and hostnames out; log them with a request id the client can quote.

visual.title: Habits for bodies
rows: Send `Content-Type: application/json`, and `Accept` when you want JSON back
Mixed styles cause bugs in every client
Not "03/14/26", not seconds here and milliseconds there
Money as integer cents (`"price_cents": 1999`) or a decimal string
Return the resource from POST, PUT and PATCH
Pagination fields can be added later without breaking anyone
Adding a field stays a safe change

sections.tip: Include a request id in every error response and in your server logs. "Quote this id to support" turns a vague bug report into a two-minute log search.
sections.pitfall: Different error shapes from different endpoints: a plain string here, `{error: ...}` there, an HTML page from the proxy on a 502. Clients end up full of special cases.

activity.title: Read a real response
activity.prompt: This is a response from GET /v1/orders. Explore the tree first: find the path to the second order's first item SKU, the type of total_cents, and the value you would send to get the next page. Notice the null gift_note, and that the list is wrapped in an object so pagination fields fit beside it. Then take the quiz.

check.question: Which is the best way to represent a price of $19.99 in a JSON API?
choices: "price_cents": 1999
"price": "19.99 dollars"
check.explanation: An integer count of cents is exact and easy to do math with. 19.99 as a JSON number is usually parsed as a float, which cannot represent most decimal amounts exactly, and a string with a unit in it has to be parsed by hand.

sections.title: Pagination, filtering and versioning
sections.key: Paginate every list: offsets are simple but slow down and shift as rows arrive, cursors stay fast and stable; and add a version only for breaking changes.
sections.body:
`GET /orders` was quick with 30 test orders. In production one customer has 2 million, the response takes 40 seconds and the app crashes. Every list needs pagination from day one.

[[visual]]

Filters and sorting go in the query string: `GET /v1/orders?status=shipped&sort=-created_at`. Check fields against an allowlist, and cap `limit` on the server.

**Versioning** exists because clients you do not control keep calling old shapes for years. Most APIs put it in the path (`/v1/orders`); some use a header such as `API-Version: 2026-03-01`. Knowing what breaks matters more:

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

items.title: Offset
points: `offset` counts rows skipped: `offset=50` starts at item 51
Simple; users can jump to page 7
The database walks past every skipped row, so deep pages get slow
Inserts shift rows: items seen twice or missed

items.title: Cursor (keyset)
points: An opaque `next_cursor` encodes where the last page ended
The next query seeks through an index: fast at any depth
New rows do not shift pages
No jumping to page 7; feeds, chat and exports use it

items.title: Safe to add in v1
points: An optional response field
A new optional query parameter
A new endpoint

items.title: Breaking
items.sub: new version, or a long deprecation
points: Removing or renaming a field
Changing a field's type
Making an optional input required
Changing what a status means

sections.deeper:
Behind a cursor, the server's next query is roughly `WHERE (created_at, id) < (last_created_at, last_id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 25`. An index answers that directly, however deep the page.

Offset arithmetic: with `limit=25`, items 51 to 75 are `offset=50`, because the offset counts the rows skipped.

Header versioning keeps URLs clean, but is harder to try in a browser; dated versions such as `API-Version: 2026-03-01` are popular with payment APIs.
sections.tip: Make cursors opaque (for example base64 of the last id and timestamp) so clients cannot build them by hand, and you stay free to change what is inside.
sections.pitfall: Offset pagination over a table that is written to constantly. Users see the same item twice or miss one entirely as rows shift between requests.

check.question: A chat app loads older messages as you scroll up, while new messages arrive constantly. Which pagination fits best?
choices: Offset pagination with page numbers
Returning every message and paginating in the client
Cursor pagination keyed on the last message's timestamp and id
Offset pagination with a larger page size
check.explanation: New messages would shift offsets and cause duplicates or gaps. A cursor marks exactly where the last page ended, so inserts do not disturb it, and the index lookup stays fast however far back you scroll.

sections.title: Authentication: sessions, tokens, API keys and OAuth
sections.key: Sessions suit browser apps on the same site, bearer tokens suit mobile and cross-domain clients, API keys suit servers, and OAuth lets users grant limited access.
sections.body:
Three clients call your API: your web app, your mobile app and a partner's server syncing orders hourly. They need different mechanisms.

[[visual]]

A **JWT** is a base64url header and payload plus a signature. Any server can verify it without a lookup, but the payload is only encoded, not encrypted: anyone holding the token can read it. Keep JWTs short-lived, with a refresh token.

**OAuth 2.0** lets a user grant your app limited access (**scopes**) to their data elsewhere without sharing their password. **OpenID Connect** adds an ID token saying who the user is: "Sign in with Google".

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: Which credential
rows: A browser app on the same site as its API. A random id in an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite` cookie; log out by deleting the session
Mobile apps and browser apps calling other domains: `Authorization: Bearer <token>`
Server to server, identifying an application. A long-lived secret: servers and secret managers only, never frontend code or app bundles
A user delegating access to their data on another service; the authorization code flow with PKCE

visual.title: OAuth authorization code flow with PKCE

messages.label: Log in, approve scopes
messages.detail: your app never sees the password

messages.label: Redirect with a short code
messages.detail: and the state, which the app checks

sections.deeper:
OAuth is about authorization: what the app may do, expressed as scopes such as `read:user`. Authentication (who are you?) and authorization (what may you do?) are separate questions, and the API must check both on every request.

Always use HTTPS, and never put credentials in URLs: they end up in server logs and browser history.

The `state` value protects against forged redirects, and PKCE (the code challenge and verifier) stops a stolen authorization code from being exchanged by anyone but the app that started the flow.
sections.tip: In the browser, prefer an HttpOnly cookie over localStorage for tokens. Any script on the page can read localStorage, including one injected through an XSS bug.
sections.pitfall: Putting an API key in frontend JavaScript or a mobile app and assuming it is hidden. Anything shipped to a device can be extracted; keep secret keys on your server.

activity.title: Who are you, and are you allowed?
activity.prompt: Call GET /api/me with no token and read the 401. Log in to get a token, then call /api/me again with an Authorization: Bearer header. Finally, try GET /api/admin/stats with the same token. Notice the difference: 401 means prove who you are, 403 means you are known but not allowed.

check.question: Your server needs to pull invoices every night from a payment provider using your company's own account. No end user is involved. What do you most likely use?
choices: An OAuth flow in which a user approves access every night
A session cookie copied from logging in to the provider's website
A JWT generated by your frontend
A secret API key stored on your server
check.explanation: Server-to-server calls on your own account are what API keys are for. OAuth exists so a user can delegate access, and a copied website cookie or a frontend-made token is fragile and insecure.

sections.title: Rate limits, retries and idempotency keys
sections.key: Clients honor Retry-After, back off exponentially with jitter, retry only errors that can pass later, and reuse one idempotency key across every attempt.
sections.body:
Your backfill script calls an API as fast as it can, and soon every request fails with **429 Too Many Requests**. The server counts requests per key, user or IP and rejects the excess, often with `Retry-After: 30` and headers such as `X-RateLimit-Remaining`.

[[visual]]

Where real money gets lost: `POST /payments` times out. Did the charge happen? Retrying may charge twice; not retrying may lose the sale. The fix is an **idempotency key**: one UUID per logical operation, sent on every attempt. The server stores the first result under that key and returns it for repeats.

[[code]]

visual.title: Retrying well
rows: Wait and retry; honor `Retry-After` when sent
Possibly temporary: retry if the request is idempotent or carries an idempotency key
Never retry automatically: it fails the same way
**Exponential backoff**: 1, 2, 4, 8 seconds up to a cap, then give up
Add random **jitter**, so they do not all retry at the same instant

sections.tip: Generate the idempotency key once per logical operation, outside the retry loop. A new key on every attempt defeats the purpose.
sections.pitfall: Retrying immediately in a tight loop. It turns a brief overload into a full outage, and can get your API key blocked.

check.question: Why add random jitter to exponential backoff?
choices: To make each retry look like a new client to the rate limiter
To make the total wait shorter than plain backoff
Because Retry-After values are always approximate
To spread out retries from many clients so they do not all arrive at the same instant
check.explanation: Clients that failed together would otherwise retry together, creating synchronized spikes that keep a recovering server down. Jitter does not shorten the wait or hide the client from the limiter.

sections.title: Calling APIs from Python and JavaScript
sections.key: Clients must set timeouts, check the status before reading the body, and send JSON correctly: requests has `json=` and no default timeout, and fetch resolves on 404 and 500.
sections.body:
Most API bugs are in clients that assume every call succeeds.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

Notice how a 422 becomes data the form can use, while other failures become exceptions with enough detail (method, id, status) to debug from one log line.

items.title: Python: requests
points: `params={...}` builds and encodes the query string
`json=payload` serializes and sets Content-Type; `data=` sends a form body instead
Always pass `timeout`: there is no default
`r.raise_for_status()` before `r.json()`
Catch `requests.RequestException`; reuse a `requests.Session()`

items.title: JavaScript: fetch
points: Rejects only when no response arrives: network, DNS, CORS, abort
A 404 or 500 resolves: check `res.ok` or `res.status`
`res.json()` returns a promise: await it
No default timeout: `AbortSignal.timeout(5000)`
`body: JSON.stringify(obj)` plus the Content-Type header, yourself

sections.tip: Log the method, URL (without secrets), status and a snippet of the body for every failed call. "Request failed" with no details turns a five-minute fix into an afternoon.
sections.pitfall: Writing `await fetch(url).json()`. `.json()` is then called on the promise, not the response, and throws a TypeError; write `(await fetch(url)).json()` or use two lines.

check.question: `fetch('/api/orders/999')` gets a 404 response from the server. What happens?
choices: The promise rejects with a 404 error
The promise resolves with a Response whose ok property is false
The promise never settles
fetch retries the request three times, then rejects
check.explanation: fetch treats any HTTP response, including 404 and 500, as a successful request. It only rejects on network-level failures or an abort, so checking res.ok is your job.

sections.title: Beyond REST: GraphQL and gRPC
sections.key: GraphQL lets a client fetch exactly the nested fields it needs in one request, but caching and monitoring get harder; gRPC gives fast, typed calls between internal services.
sections.body:
A mobile home screen needs the user's name, their last three orders and each order's first item image. With REST that is four or five round trips (**under-fetching**), each carrying fields the screen ignores (**over-fetching**).

[[visual]]

[[code]]

Rule of thumb: REST for public, general-purpose APIs (everyone knows it, and caching and tooling are excellent), GraphQL when many clients need flexible views of connected data, gRPC for high-volume internal calls between services you control. Plenty of companies run all three.

items.title: REST
points: Resources at URLs with standard methods
Excellent HTTP caching and tooling
A screen may need several round trips

items.title: GraphQL
points: One endpoint (`POST /graphql`) and a typed schema
The client names exactly the nested fields it wants
Harder HTTP caching; errors come back as **200** with an `errors` array
Needs query cost limits, and batching (DataLoader) against N+1

items.title: gRPC
points: Services and messages in a `.proto` file; generated clients
HTTP/2, binary **Protocol Buffers**, streaming both ways
Fast and typed, but not human-readable; browsers need gRPC-Web

sections.deeper:
A gRPC service definition looks like `service Orders { rpc GetOrder (GetOrderRequest) returns (Order); }`, and the compiler generates client and server code in many languages, so a remote call reads like a local function call.

GraphQL's schema doubles as documentation, and frontend teams can change what they fetch without waiting for a backend change. Naive resolvers load related data one row at a time, which is the N+1 problem again.
sections.tip: In interviews, "why not GraphQL?" is a trade-off question. Name one gain (fewer round trips, exact fields) and one cost (harder caching, query cost limits).
sections.pitfall: Alerting only on HTTP 5xx for a GraphQL API. Most GraphQL errors arrive as 200 responses with an errors array.

check.question: Which situation fits gRPC best?
choices: A public API that third-party developers explore with curl
A static marketing site served from a CDN
High-volume calls between internal services written in Go and Java
A browser app calling the backend directly with no proxy in between
check.explanation: gRPC shines between services you control: generated typed clients in many languages, compact binary messages and streaming. Browsers need a gRPC-Web proxy, and binary payloads make it awkward for public developers using curl.

keyTerms.definition: A noun the API exposes at a URL, such as /orders or /orders/42, acted on with HTTP methods.
Sending the request once or many times leaves the server in the same state. GET, PUT and DELETE are; POST is not.
A method that only reads and never changes server state: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS.
A standard JSON error shape (RFC 9457) with type, title, status and detail fields.
Paging with an opaque token marking where the last page ended; fast at any depth and stable under inserts.
A credential sent as Authorization: Bearer <token>; whoever holds it can use it.
A signed token whose base64url payload anyone can read; the signature only proves it was not altered.
A long-lived secret identifying a calling application, meant for server-side use.
A protocol that lets a user grant an app scoped access to their data elsewhere without sharing a password.
A unique id sent with a non-idempotent request so the server can recognize retries and not repeat the action.
Retrying after waits that double each time, usually with random jitter and a cap.
A query language and single endpoint where the client asks for exactly the fields it needs.

summary: Resources are nouns and methods are verbs; GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, POST is not.
401 authenticate, 403 not allowed, 422 fix the fields, 429 and 503 wait and retry.
One JSON error shape, cursor pagination for big lists, new versions only for breaking changes.
Sessions for same-site browsers, tokens for mobile, API keys for servers, OAuth for delegation.
Set timeouts, check statuses, back off with jitter, reuse one idempotency key.
GraphQL trades caching for flexible queries; gRPC trades readability for fast typed calls.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a new teammate why retrying a timed-out POST /payments can charge a customer twice, and how idempotence and an idempotency key prevent it.

questions.question: Which request follows REST conventions for reading order 42?
choices: GET /getOrder?id=42
POST /orders/read/42
GET /orders/42
GET /order.json?orderId=42
questions.explanation: The resource is the order, addressed as an item in the orders collection, and the method (GET) says what you are doing. The other options put verbs or file extensions in the path or misuse POST for a read.

questions.question: Which HTTP methods are idempotent according to the HTTP specification? Select all that apply.
choices: GET
POST
PUT
DELETE
HEAD
PATCH
questions.explanation: GET and HEAD are safe, so repeating them changes nothing. PUT sets a resource to a given state, and DELETE leaves it deleted, no matter how many times you send them. POST creates something new each time, and PATCH is not guaranteed to be idempotent (a patch can say 'add 1').

questions.question: A client sends `DELETE /orders/42` and gets 204. Its retry logic sends it again and gets 404. A teammate says this proves DELETE is not idempotent. What is the best reply?
choices: They are right: an idempotent method must return the same status every time
Idempotence is about server state, and the order is deleted either way, so DELETE is still idempotent
DELETE is only idempotent when the server returns 204 both times
The retry should have used PUT, which is the idempotent way to delete
questions.explanation: Idempotence describes the effect on server state, not the response. After one DELETE or two, order 42 is gone, so the method is idempotent even though the second response differs.

questions.question: What is the difference between `PUT /users/7` and `PATCH /users/7`?
choices: PUT creates a new user, while PATCH updates an existing one
PUT is for admins, while PATCH is for regular users
They are interchangeable names for the same operation
PUT replaces the whole user with the body, while PATCH changes only the fields sent
questions.explanation: PUT sends the complete new representation and replaces what is there; PATCH sends only the changes. A PUT that leaves out a field may clear it, which surprises people who meant to PATCH.

questions.question: Match each status code to the situation it describes.

pairs.right: POST /orders worked and the new order has an id
DELETE worked and there is nothing to return
The ETag sent in If-None-Match still matches
Signing up with a username that is already taken
The client went over 100 requests per minute
The server is overloaded and asks you to come back later

questions.explanation: 201 and 204 are successes with and without a body to return, 304 answers a conditional GET, 409 is a clash with current state, 429 is rate limiting, and 503 is temporary unavailability.

questions.question: A request returns 401 Unauthorized. What should a well-behaved client do?
choices: Show 'You do not have permission' and never retry
Get fresh credentials (refresh the token or ask the user to log in), then try again
Retry the identical request with exponential backoff
Switch the request from GET to POST
questions.explanation: 401 means the server could not authenticate the request: the token is missing, expired or invalid. Refreshing the token or logging in again can fix it. Showing 'no permission' is the response to 403, and repeating the same request unchanged just gets another 401.

questions.question: The server receives this request. The JSON parses fine, but the email is not a valid address. Which response fits best?
choices: 400 Bad Request, because the JSON syntax is invalid
422 Unprocessable Content, because the body is well-formed but fails validation
409 Conflict, because the email conflicts with the expected format
415 Unsupported Media Type, because the email is not a real address
questions.explanation: The body is well-formed JSON, so it is not a syntax problem. It fails validation, which is what 422 describes. (Some APIs use 400 for validation errors too, but the reason given in that choice, invalid JSON syntax, is wrong here.)

questions.question: After a deploy, your service returns 500 for some requests. During a planned database failover, it returns 503 with Retry-After. How should a client's retry logic treat these?
choices: Retry both forever until they succeed
Never retry either, because 5xx errors are always permanent
Retry 503 after waiting, honoring Retry-After; retry a 500 at most once or twice, then report the error
Retry 500 aggressively, since 503 means the endpoint has been removed
questions.explanation: 503 explicitly means 'temporarily unavailable', so waiting (honoring Retry-After) and retrying makes sense. A 500 usually means a bug that the same request will hit again; a retry or two is fine for idempotent requests, but then surface the error.

questions.question: Your `POST /orders` handler creates order 1043 and returns 201. Which response header should give the client the URL of the new order?
questions.explanation: A 201 response should include a Location header such as `Location: /v1/orders/1043`, so the client knows where the new resource lives.

questions.question: Clients say their 'order not found' handling never runs. What is wrong with this Express handler?
choices: res.json cannot send an object that has an error key
findById returns a promise, so order is always truthy
The route must use POST in order to return errors
The missing order is sent with status 200, so clients that check the status see a success
questions.explanation: res.json sends status 200 unless you set another one, so the client sees a success with an odd body. It should be `res.status(404).json({...})`. findById is awaited, so order is a real value, not a promise.

questions.question: A signup form receives this response. The form wants to show each message under the matching input. What should the client code use?
choices: The errors array, matching each entry's field to an input
The title string, split into words
The status number, mapped to a list of known fields
The type URL, downloaded and parsed at runtime
questions.explanation: The errors array is structured for exactly this: each entry names a field and a message. Parsing the human title is fragile, and status and type only say that validation failed, not which field.

questions.question: Why should a list endpoint return `{"data": [...]}` instead of a bare JSON array?
choices: JSON does not allow arrays at the top level
So pagination fields such as next_cursor can be added later without breaking clients
Arrays are much slower to parse than objects
So the status code can be repeated inside the body
questions.explanation: An object leaves room for next_cursor, has_more or totals later without changing the response type. JSON does allow a top-level array; the problem is that you cannot add fields to one without breaking clients.

questions.question: Orders are sorted newest first. A user loads `?limit=20&offset=0`, and before they load `?limit=20&offset=20`, three new orders are created. What does page 2 show?
choices: The last three orders from page 1 appear again at the top of page 2
Page 2 silently skips three orders
Exactly the same orders as before; offsets are stable
The API returns 409 Conflict because the data changed
questions.explanation: The three new orders push every existing order down three places, so the first three rows at offset 20 are the last three rows the user already saw on page 1. Cursor pagination avoids this.

questions.question: With `limit=25`, which offset returns items 51 to 75 (counting the first item as 1)?
questions.explanation: Offsets count how many items to skip. Skipping 50 items starts the page at item 51, and 25 items later it ends at 75.

questions.question: Your public API is at v1. Which changes can ship without a new version? Select all that apply.
choices: Adding an optional gift_note field to order responses
Renaming total_cents to total
Adding an optional ?currency= query parameter
Making the optional phone field required on POST /orders
Changing id from a number to a string
Adding a new endpoint, GET /v1/refunds
questions.explanation: Additions that clients can ignore are safe: an optional response field, an optional parameter, a new endpoint. Renaming a field, changing a type or making an input required breaks existing clients.

questions.question: Why do cursor-based pages stay fast at any depth, while large offsets get slower and slower?
choices: Cursor responses are cached by the CDN, while offset responses are not
Large offsets lock the whole table while they run
The database seeks straight to the last-seen key through an index, instead of walking past every skipped row
Cursor responses are compressed, while offset responses are sent raw
questions.explanation: A cursor becomes a WHERE condition on an indexed key, so the database jumps straight to the right spot. OFFSET 500000 makes it produce and throw away half a million rows first. Caching and compression have nothing to do with it.

questions.question: Your React app is served from shop.example.com and its API lives at shop.example.com/api. Which authentication approach is the most natural fit?
choices: A session id in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie
An API key embedded in the JavaScript bundle
OAuth, so the user can grant the site access to itself
HTTP Basic auth with the password in the URL
questions.explanation: Same-site browser apps are what session cookies were made for. Marked HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite, the cookie is sent automatically and scripts cannot read it. An API key in the bundle is public, and OAuth is for delegating access to another service.

questions.question: A teammate puts each user's tax id in the JWT payload, saying 'it's fine, the token is signed'. Given this exhibit, what is the problem?
choices: JWT payloads may only contain numbers, so the token is invalid
The signature makes tokens too large to send in a header
Signing stops tampering but not reading: anyone holding the token can decode the payload
Nothing is wrong, because a signed token is also encrypted
questions.explanation: A JWT signature proves the token was not tampered with, but the payload is just base64url-encoded JSON. Anyone who gets the token (logs, browser storage, a proxy) can read it. Keep sensitive data out of JWTs or use an encrypted format.

questions.question: Put the steps of the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow (with PKCE) in order.
items: Your app redirects the user to the provider's authorize page with the scopes it wants
The user logs in at the provider and approves those scopes
The provider redirects back to your app with a short-lived authorization code
Your app exchanges the code, plus the PKCE verifier, for an access token
Your app calls the provider's API with the access token as a bearer token
questions.explanation: The user approves access at the provider, not in your app. Your app receives only a short-lived code, exchanges it (with the PKCE verifier) for an access token, and uses that token for API calls.

questions.question: What problem does OAuth 2.0 solve, and what does OpenID Connect add?
questions.answer: OAuth 2.0 lets a user grant an app limited, revocable access (scopes) to their data on another service without sharing their password: it is about authorization. OpenID Connect adds an ID token on top, so the app also learns who the user is (authentication).
questions.explanation: Interviewers like this distinction because many people say 'OAuth login'. OAuth grants access; OpenID Connect proves identity.

questions.question: A developer puts the company's secret payment API key in the React frontend so the browser can call the provider directly. What is the problem?
choices: Browsers block every request that includes an API key
Anyone can read the key from the bundle and make calls as your company
The key expires as soon as the page reloads
React removes custom headers from outgoing requests
questions.explanation: Everything in a JavaScript bundle is downloadable and readable. Anyone can pull out the key and make calls as your company. Keep secret keys on the server and have the frontend call your own API.

questions.question: Customers are occasionally charged twice by this function. What is the bug?
choices: The 10 second timeout is too long for a payment API
raise_for_status must be called after r.json()
A new idempotency key is made for every attempt, so the server cannot recognize a retry of the same charge
2 ** attempt grows too quickly and overflows
questions.explanation: After a timeout the first charge may already have gone through. Because each attempt sends a brand-new key, the server sees the retry as a new charge. Create the key once, before the loop, and send the same key on every attempt.

questions.question: Which of these should an API client retry automatically, after a wait? Select all that apply.
choices: 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After: 10
503 Service Unavailable
A timeout on GET /v1/orders
400 Bad Request
403 Forbidden
422 Unprocessable Content
questions.explanation: 429, 503 and a timeout on an idempotent GET can all succeed later. 400, 403 and 422 describe a problem with the request or the user's permissions, so the same request will fail the same way.

questions.question: A client uses exponential backoff that waits 1 second before the first retry and doubles each time (1, 2, 4, ...), with no cap and no jitter. How many seconds does it wait before the 5th retry?
questions.explanation: The waits are 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds, so the 5th retry waits 16 seconds. That rapid growth is why real clients add a cap.

questions.question: When the session expires, the API returns 401 with `{"title": "Unauthorized"}`, and this page renders an empty profile instead of the error message. Why?
choices: fetch resolves on a 401, and the code never checks res.ok, so the error body is rendered as a profile
fetch rejects on 401, but the catch block is skipped inside async functions
res.json() cannot parse error bodies, so it returns an empty object
await cannot be used inside a try block
questions.explanation: fetch resolves for any HTTP response, including 401. The code never checks res.ok, so the error body is parsed and rendered as if it were a profile. Add `if (!res.ok) throw ...` before res.json().

questions.question: The server answers this request with 404. What is logged?
choices: true 404
undefined 404
Nothing: it throws before logging
false 404
questions.explanation: fetch resolves with a Response for a 404; ok is false because the status is outside 200 to 299. Nothing throws.

questions.question: Complete the fetch call so it sends the `order` object as a JSON body.
choices: order
JSON.stringify(order)
JSON.parse(order)
order.toString()
questions.explanation: fetch sends the body as given and does not serialize objects, so you convert with JSON.stringify. Passing the object directly sends the string "[object Object]".

questions.question: Complete the call so requests sends the dict `order` as a JSON body.
choices: data
params
json
body
questions.explanation: The json= argument serializes the dict and sets Content-Type: application/json. data= sends a form-encoded body, params= puts values in the query string, and body= is not a requests argument at all.

questions.question: A nightly job that calls this function sometimes runs for nine hours and never finishes. What is the most likely cause?
questions.code:
def fetch_rates():
    r = requests.get("https://rates.example.com/latest")
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()["rates"]
choices: raise_for_status keeps retrying until the request succeeds
No timeout is set, so a server that never answers blocks the call forever
r.json() downloads the whole response again each time it is called
requests retries failed requests forever by default
questions.explanation: requests has no default timeout. If the server accepts the connection and then never responds, the call blocks forever. Pass timeout=(connect, read) seconds, for example timeout=10. requests does not retry on its own by default.

questions.question: A mobile home screen needs the user's name, their last 3 orders and each order's first item image. With the REST API this takes 5 round trips. Which approach addresses this most directly?
choices: gRPC streaming from the phone to the server
Switching the responses from JSON to XML
A GraphQL query that names exactly the nested fields the screen needs
Moving the REST API to /v2
questions.explanation: GraphQL lets the client ask for exactly these nested fields in one request. gRPC is aimed at service-to-service calls, and changing formats or versions does not reduce round trips.

questions.question: Match each technology to its description.

pairs.right: Resources at URLs with standard methods and easy HTTP caching
One endpoint where the client names exactly the fields it wants
Service-to-service calls over HTTP/2 with streaming and generated clients
The .proto schema language and its compact binary encoding

questions.explanation: REST is resource URLs plus HTTP methods, GraphQL is one endpoint with client-chosen fields, gRPC is typed service calls over HTTP/2, and Protocol Buffers are the schema and binary format gRPC uses.

questions.question: Your GraphQL API's dashboard shows a 0% error rate, yet users report failures every day. What is the most likely reason?
choices: GraphQL errors are returned with status 200 in an errors array, and the dashboard only counts 5xx responses
GraphQL has no way to report errors, so they are silently dropped
The CDN is caching error responses and serving them as successes
gRPC is intercepting and swallowing the errors before they are logged
questions.explanation: GraphQL servers usually answer with 200 and report problems in an errors array in the body. A dashboard that only counts 5xx responses never sees them. Track the errors array as its own metric.
